references.text: The immediate context: The master of the house has shut the door, and they stand outside knocking, saying, 'Lord, open for us!' – but he answers, 'I do not know where you come from' ([ref:Luk 13:25|Luke 13:25]). Verse 26 describes the excluded ones' attempt to justify themselves.

A parallel in the Sermon on the Mount where many will say on judgment day, 'Lord, Lord! Did we not prophesy in your name … and do many mighty works?' – but Jesus answers, 'I never knew you' ([ref:Matt 7:22-23|Matthew 7:22-23]). The same pattern: claiming fellowship with Jesus, yet being rejected.

In the parable of the ten virgins, the foolish ones cry out, 'Lord, Lord, open for us!' but the bridegroom answers, 'I do not know you' ([ref:Matt 25:11-12|Matthew 25:11-12]). The motif of a shut door and rejection despite claimed acquaintance is common.

The following verse where the Lord responds with final rejection: 'Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity!' ([ref:Luk 13:27|Luke 13:27]). Having eaten and drunk with Jesus and heard him teach is not enough without true repentance.

People will come from east and west, north and south and sit at the table in God's kingdom ([ref:Luk 13:29|Luke 13:29]), while those who claimed fellowship at the table with Jesus are cast out – an ironic contrast.

Paul notes that all the Israelites ate the same spiritual food and drank the same spiritual drink ([ref:1 Kor 10:3-4|1 Corinthians 10:3-4]), yet God was not pleased with most of them. Sharing a meal in God's presence does not guarantee salvation.

Jesus warns the cities of Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum, which experienced his miracles and teaching but did not repent ([ref:Matt 11:21-24|Matthew 11:21-24]). Proximity to Jesus' work without repentance leads to a stricter judgment.

Jesus tells the crowd that they seek him because they were filled with bread, not because they saw the signs ([ref:Joh 6:26-27|John 6:26-27]). External fellowship at the table with Jesus without faith is insufficient.
About those who 'confess that they know God, but deny him by their works' ([ref:Tit 1:16|Titus 1:16]). Claiming to know the Lord without it being reflected in one's life is futile.

God rebukes those who steal, murder, and practice idolatry, only to then come to the temple and say, 'We are saved!' ([ref:Jer 7:8-11|Jeremiah 7:8-11]). Claiming God's presence without repentance gives false security – a motif underlying Jesus' warning.
